SKLB-39b exhibits over 100-fold selectivity for BRD4-BD1 relative to BRD4-BD2 and nearly 10-fold greater affinity for BRD4-BD1 than for BRD2/3-BD1. Mechanistically, we identify a BRD4-BD1-p62 interaction that links BET bromodomain function to autophagy regulation. By engaging Leu92 and Ile146 through a hydrophobic binding mode, SKLB-39b disrupts this interaction, restores ULK1-dependent autophagy, and provides a structural framework for BD1-selective inhibitor design. SKLB-39b outperformed JQ-1 in suppressing fibroblast activation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and collagen deposition in experimental fibrosis while showing favorable pharmacokinetic exposure and no overt toxicity in the mouse studies performed. These findings establish the BRD4-BD1-p62 interface as a druggable target for restoring protective autophagy in IPF.

title: A modular platform for in cellulo target engagement profiling of chromatin reader inhibitors
abstract: The dysregulation of acylation-reading bromodomain proteins is implicated in many diseases, making them important therapeutic targets. However, drug development is hindered by a lack of high-throughput cellular assays to measure target engagement and off-target binding in living cells. To address this gap, we developed a panel of cell lines that express synthetic bromodomain constructs, termed Acyl-eCRs. We demonstrate that Acyl-eCRs recapitulate the same response to bromodomain inhibitors and PROTACs as endogenous proteins, allowing for quantitative assessment of drug effects. We introduce two complementary flow cytometry-based assays to evaluate inhibitor-target engagement: a competitive binding assay leveraging PROTAC-induced degradation, and a nuclear retention assay measuring displacement of bromodomains from chromatin. Our approach circumvents laborious protein purification and in vitro characterization, providing a scalable, physiologically relevant method for assessing inhibitor potency and specificity. This platform provides a scalable strategy for quantitative target-engagement profiling of chromatin reader inhibitors in living cells.

title: Disease-causing helix-8 mutations reprogram parathyroid hormone receptor-1 effector selectivity
abstract: Helix-8 is an important determinant of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) effector selectivity, yet its functional relevance and contribution to human disease remain poorly understood. Two helix-8 mutations in parathyroid hormone receptor-1 (PTH1R), E465 8.49 K and E469 8.53 K, cause skeletal dysplasia, but their mechanistic effects on signaling were unclear. Using live-cell biosensors, structural modeling, and humanized knock-in mice, we show that these mutants reconfigure polar networks at the receptor's cytoplasmic face to reshape effector coupling. E465K shifts PTH1R signaling away from Gαs toward Gαq activation, causing a switch in G protein selectivity. E469K stabilizes βarrestin engagement and enhances GRK2 recruitment, to thereby competitively limit G protein signaling. E469K-PTH1R mice show impaired calcemic responses to PTH, which are restored by a βarrestin-deficient PTH analog. These findings establish helix-8 as a critical determinant of GPCR effector selectivity and reveal mutation-driven rewiring of receptor signaling as a mechanism underlying PTH1R-associated disease.

title: Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection
abstract: Cas13a enzymes are particularly attractive for nucleic acid detection due to their robust collateral activity. Recently, there has been a surge in the discovery and engineering of thermostable Cas13a proteins for nucleic acid detection. The thermostable Cas13a from Thermoclostridium caenicola (TccCas13a) was identified; however, its native target sensitivity and collateral activity are relatively low and require optimization for molecular diagnostic applications. Here, we report comprehensive biochemical characterization and structure-guided engineering of TccCas13a. Our analyses reveal its intrinsic thermostability, nucleotide substrate preferences, and tolerance to structured target RNA substrates. Rational engineering of the spacer-target RNA binding channel improved target engagement and enabled determination of a 3.13 Å cryo-electron microscopy ternary structure. Furthermore, extensive structure-guided engineering of active site-proximal regions yielded a variant with over ∼100-fold enhanced target sensitivity and collateral activity across diverse biological matrices. Together, our work provides mechanistic insights and establishes TccCas13a as a platform for next-generation RNA diagnostics.

title: Location, location, deUFMylation: Coordinating ribosome quality control at the ER
abstract: Endoplasmic-reticulum-associated ribosome quality control (ER-RQC) requires ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) for UFMylation of the ribosomal protein RPL26. In the August 6 issue of Molecular Cell, Mao et al. 1 identify an ER-associated complex (UFSP2/ODR4) as critical for deUFMylation of RPL26 and uncover a critical physiologic role for UFSP2 in neuronal proteostasis.

title: Targeting protein arginine methyltransferases to enhance cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Arginine methylation is a post-translational modification found on many proteins, including RNA-binding proteins, signaling molecules, histones, and heat shock proteins, where it can alter protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. Arginine methylation regulates many cellular pathways, including RNA metabolism, signal transduction, gene expression, cellular stress responses, DNA repair, and, more recently, innate immune sensing. Here, we discuss recent advances in innate immune sensing and the emerging role of arginine methylation in suppressing tumor immune visibility. We describe current knowledge of protein arginine methyltransferase (PRMT) inhibitors and degraders and their use from preclinical models to clinical trials, alone or in combination with other therapies, to reduce tumor progression and enhance the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy.

title: Protein arginine methylation rewires molecular interactions
abstract: Protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMT1-9) catalyze monomethylation and dimethylation of arginine residues in RNA- and DNA-associated proteins. Protein arginine methylation can weaken or strengthen nucleic acid binding, recruit or exclude protein partners, and promote or suppress higher-order assembly, making its molecular consequences highly context dependent. Methylation preserves the cationic character of the guanidinium group, while altering hydrogen-bond donor topology, steric accessibility, and interaction geometry. These effects are particularly consequential in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), where arginine-rich motifs mediate multivalent protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. Here, we propose an interaction-equilibrium framework in which arginine methylation redistributes binding capacity among the competing protein, nucleic acid, and assembly states. This framework integrates reader-dependent and reader-independent effects of methylarginine and provides a chemical basis for understanding how a charge-preserving modification can reweight molecular interactions across diverse cellular contexts.

title: Meet the authors: Cameron Douglas and Ciaran Seath
abstract: In an interview with Samantha Nelson, a scientific editor of Cell Chemical Biology, the authors of the review entitled "Chemical biology tools for studying histone post-translational modifications" share their perspectives on their field and life as scientists.

title: Meet the authors: Song-Iee Han and Akiyoshi Fukamizu
abstract: In an interview with Samantha Nelson, a scientific editor of Cell Chemical Biology, the authors of the review entitled "Arginine methylation in immunoregulation: mechanisms and therapeutic targeting" reflect on advances in their field, their scientific journeys, and the experiences that have shaped their research.

title: The expanding biology of post-translational modifications
abstract: In this editorial, guest editor George Burslem and the Cell Chemical Biology editorial team introduce a special issue from Cell Chemical Biology on post-translational modifications! They present a collection of articles including several reviews, a primer, a spotlight, and various opinion pieces from a community of scientists studying the chemical biology of post-translational modifications.

title: Voices: Emerging molecular mechanisms and open questions in post-translational modifications
abstract: Post-translational modifications expand the functional diversity of the proteome and provide dynamic control over protein activity, localization, interactions, and stability, making them fundamental regulators of cellular function. In this Voices piece accompanying a special issue on post-translational modifications in Cell Chemical Biology, we ask researchers from across the field: what recent advances in post-translational modification research are most exciting, what important challenges remain, and what are the next big questions for the field?

title: Selective USP32 inhibition reveals endosomal ubiquitin signaling and enables cell-permeable activity-based probes
abstract: Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) regulate ubiquitin signaling and are attractive therapeutic targets, but selective chemical tools remain available for only a limited number of family members. Here, we report Huib32, the first potent and selective covalent inhibitor of ubiquitin-specific protease 32 (USP32). Huib32 rapidly and selectively engages USP32 in vitro and in cells, recapitulating USP32 loss of function by enhancing substrate ubiquitination, disrupting endosomal organization, and defining an expanded network of USP32-regulated membrane trafficking proteins. Building on Huib32, we develop the first cell-permeable activity-based probes for USP32, enabling direct visualization of active USP32 in cells and selective proteomic enrichment of the enzyme. Together, these first-in-class chemical tools establish selective chemical targeting of USP32 as an approach to interrogate endosomal ubiquitin signaling and provide a foundation for therapeutic exploration in cancers and other diseases associated with endocytic trafficking.

title: Small-molecule modulation of VDAC enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by promoting ATP flux
abstract: Reduced insulin secretion by β cells is a pivotal factor in diabetes onset and progression. The small molecule NPD976 was identified as a potent insulin secretagogue using high-throughput chemical screening employing an insulin secretion assay system. Even part of the molecular structure of NPD976, designated as DPEU (N-[2-(3,4-dimethoxyphenyl)ethyl]urea), retains insulin secretagogue activity. DPEU enhances insulin secretion specifically under glucose stimulation in β cells derived from mice, rats, and humans. The compound localizes to mitochondria in a manner independent of high glucose stimulation. Biochemical analyses revealed that DPEU directly interacts with voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs) located in the mitochondrial outer membrane, enhancing ATP efflux from mitochondria into the cytosol during glucose stimulation. To our knowledge, DPEU is a positive small-molecule modulator of VDAC function that promotes ATP flux in β cells through a mechanism distinct from the classical KATP or cAMP pathways. These findings identify VDAC as a potential target for enhancing insulin secretion.

title: Proteasome inhibition bidirectionally regulates ferroptosis sensitivity
abstract: Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic cell death mechanism whose fundamental regulation continues to be elucidated. The proteasome is an essential multiprotein complex important for protein turnover. How proteasome function regulates ferroptosis is difficult to study given that proteasome inhibition causes apoptosis. Here, we isolated the effects of proteasome inhibition on ferroptosis by combining small molecule cell death inducers, pathway-specific cell death inhibitors, and direct cell death imaging. We find that proteasome inhibition enhances sensitivity to ferroptosis induced by glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) inhibition while simultaneously promoting resistance to ferroptosis induced by system x c - inhibition. Sensitization to GPX4 inhibition requires protein synthesis but not the apoptosis execution machinery and is opposed by the activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) stress response pathway. These findings establish proteasome-mediated protein turnover as a context-dependent regulator of ferroptosis and identify protein synthesis and ATF4 as key determinants of GPX4 inhibitor sensitivity.

title: Genetic dissection of rapid proteolysis identifies TXNDC15 as a key factor of ERAD and lipid homeostasis
abstract: Biological systems face a constantly changing environment and must swiftly respond to stimuli; yet how cells sense and adapt to environmental and physiological cues is incompletely understood. Short-lived proteins can be rapidly induced upon perturbation, enabling swift activation of adaptive cellular responses. Here, leveraging genome-wide data on protein-transcript correlation, we systematically searched for rapid proteolysis substrates whose abundance reflects the activity of the underlying proteolytic machinery. Focusing on the candidate substrate ABHD2, we performed CRISPR-based genetic screens to dissect its degradation. These screens identified TXNDC15 as an essential factor in MARCHF6-mediated ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD). Mechanistically, TXNDC15 supports substrate exit and degradation from the ER via a catalysis-independent mechanism. Loss of TXNDC15 remodels the ER proteome and lipid homeostasis. Together, our work defines a missing component of ERAD and provides a generalizable strategy to decode post-translational regulatory circuits.

title: Shared α-helix chimeraffibodies enable linker-free bispecific protein design
abstract: Small protein scaffolds enable precise targeting but often rely on flexible linkers that increase conformational heterogeneity and immunogenic liabilities. Here we develop Chimeraffibodies (CABs), a linker-free bispecific scaffold class that encodes interdomain geometry through seamless α-helix sharing. CABs are designed by AlphaSync, a structure-design framework that defines domain orientation through closed-form exhaustive local rigid-body superposition and ProteinMPNN-based sequence refinement. Using HER2-binding affibody and an albumin-binding domain, we generated 861CM, which preserved parental paratopes while enforcing a defined shared-helix architecture. Structural, biophysical and cellular analyses demonstrated stable assembly, cooperative target recruitment and retained affinity, with HSA binding of ∼14.3 pM and HER2 binding of 610 pM in the albumin-bound state. In vivo imaging revealed sustained tumor localization, reduced hepatic and renal background and improved organ-to-tumor contrast. CABs establish helix sharing as a geometry-encoded strategy for generating compact, homogeneous, and pharmacokinetically optimized bispecific proteins.
